sections.title: The Yukawa Particle and the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle Revisited
objectives: Estimate the mass of a pion.

misconceptions.claim: The standard model explains every particle there is.
misconceptions.correction: It explains the particles we have found so far. Gravity is not in it, and the matter and antimatter imbalance is not explained either.

authored_exercises.stem: What is the Yukawa particle, and which force does it mediate?
authored_exercises.answer: The pion, a meson that mediates the strong nuclear force between nucleons.
solution: Yukawa proposed a particle to carry the strong force.
Its mass was estimated from the range of the force and the uncertainty principle.
The pion was later discovered and matched the prediction.

authored_exercises.stem: Why does the strong force have a very short range?
authored_exercises.answer: Its carrier, the pion, has a nonzero mass, so the uncertainty principle limits how far a virtual pion can travel.
solution: A virtual particle can exist only for a short time.
The energy-time uncertainty relation limits that time.
A massive carrier therefore gives a short range.

authored_exercises.stem: Estimate the range of the strong force if the pion mass is 140 MeV/c². Take ħc ≈ 197 MeV fm.
solution: The range is roughly $r≈\hbar/(mc)=\hbar c/(mc^{2})$ .
$r≈197MeV\cdot fm/140MeV=1.4fm$ .
The strong force therefore has a range of order 1 fm.

sections.title: The Four Basic Forces
objectives: Explain the Feynman diagram for the exchange of a virtual photon between two positive charges.
Describe the Feynman diagram for the exchange of a between a proton and a neutron.

misconceptions.claim: Gravity is the strongest of the four fundamental forces.
misconceptions.correction: Gravity is the weakest. The strong nuclear force is strongest at short range, then electromagnetism, then the weak force, and gravity is far weaker than all three.

misconceptions.claim: The electromagnetic force acts only between charges that are at rest.
misconceptions.correction: It acts between charges whether they are at rest or moving. Moving charges also produce magnetic effects, which are part of the same electromagnetic interaction.

sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source section on The Four Basic Forces has no worked example; the teaching text derives the key results and the practice set applies them.

misconceptions.claim: Particles and antiparticles are the same thing with the opposite charge.
misconceptions.correction: They have the same mass and opposite charge, and when they meet they annihilate into photons.

sections.title: Particles, Patterns, and Conservation Laws
objectives: Outline the differences between hadrons and leptons.
State the differences between mesons and baryons.

misconceptions.correction: Hadrons are composite. Baryons are made of three quarks and mesons of a quark and an antiquark. Leptons, such as the electron, are the fundamental particles in this classification.

misconceptions.claim: Mesons are a type of baryon.
misconceptions.correction: Mesons and baryons are both hadrons, but they are different. Mesons contain a quark and an antiquark, while baryons contain three quarks.

authored_exercises.stem: What is the difference between a hadron and a lepton?
authored_exercises.answer: Hadrons feel the strong force and are composite; leptons do not feel the strong force and are fundamental.
solution: Hadrons include protons, neutrons and pions.
They are made of quarks and interact through the strong force.
Leptons include electrons and neutrinos and are not made of quarks.

sections.title: Quarks: Is That All There Is?
objectives: Outline the quark composition of hadrons.
Determine quantum numbers from quark composition.

misconceptions.claim: A quark can be isolated and observed on its own.
misconceptions.correction: Quarks are confined. The strong force grows with separation, so pulling quarks apart creates new quark-antiquark pairs instead of freeing a single quark.

sections.title: GUTs: The Unification of Forces
objectives: Describe the principle of quantum chromodynamics.

misconceptions.claim: Grand unified theories have been confirmed by experiment.
misconceptions.correction: GUTs are theoretical extensions that unify the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces. They predict proton decay, which has not been observed, so they remain unconfirmed.

sec-6:exr-97.answer: a) ${Δ}^{++}(uuu)$ , so $B=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=1$ b) The $d̄$ antiquark of the ${π}^{+}$ and a $d$ quark from the proton annihilate into a gluon, leaving the three $u$ quarks that form the ${Δ}^{++}$ .
solution: b) In the diagram the $d̄$ from the ${π}^{+}$ annihilates a $d$ quark of the proton into a gluon; the remaining $uuu$ forms the ${Δ}^{++}$ .

sec-6:exr-159.stem: (a) What particle has the quark composition $ūūd̄$ ? (b) What should its decay mode be?
solution: a) Three antiquarks with charges $-2/3,-2/3,+1/3$ give total charge $-1$ and baryon number $-1$: the antiproton.
b) It is the charge-conjugate of the conjectured proton decay $p→{π}^{0}+{e}^{+}$ , so $p̄→{π}^{0}+{e}^{-}$ .
sec-6:exr-159.solution_provenance: OpenStax CNXML solution element (in file); the source wrote the antiproton as 'p-', rendered here with a proper bar

sec-6:exr-124.answer: No. Charge is conserved (-1 = -1), and muon lepton number is conserved (1 = 1), but electron lepton number is not: 0 before and +2 after.
solution: Charge: $-1=(-1)+0+0$, conserved.
Muon lepton number: $1=0+0+1$, conserved.
Electron lepton number: $0=(+1)+(+1)+0=+2$, not conserved.
The decay is therefore forbidden.
sec-6:exr-124.solution_provenance: OpenStax CNXML solution element (in file); the source answer field was the digit 1

sec-6:exr-106.answer: (a) $+1$ (b) $B=1=1+0$, $Z=-1=0+(-1)$, all lepton numbers are 0 before and after (c) $(sss)→(uds)+(ūs)$
solution: (a) The ${Ω}^{-}$ has strangeness $-3$ and charge $-1$; the final state has $S=-1+(-1)=-2$ and charge $0+(-1)=-1$.
(b) Baryon number: $1=1+0$. Charge: $-1=0+(-1)$. All lepton numbers are zero on both sides.
(c) $(sss)→(uds)+(ūs)$.

sec-4:exr-33.stem: A $\pi^{+}$ and a $\pi^{-}$ are moving toward each other extremely slowly. When they collide, two $\pi^{0}$ are produced. How fast are they going? Ignore relativistic effects.
solution: The charged pions annihilate into two neutral pions. The small mass difference becomes kinetic energy, shared equally by the two products.
The mass difference is about $2(139.6)-2(135.0)=9.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so each $\pi^{0}$ gets about 4.6 MeV. This corresponds to a speed of about $7.8\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s}$.
